parole.significato: Genista tridentata, a plant native to the Iberian peninsula
parole.testo: From substrate *carcasia, *querquesia, or similar, from Celtic, from Proto-Indo-European *pérkus ~ *pr̥kʷéu- (“oak”). Compare the local pre-Roman tribal name Querquerni abd Galician carqueixa.

parole.significato: top of a conical structure, heap or mountain
parole.testo: Attested since the 12th century, in Latin charters. Probably from a substrate language; compare Proto-Celtic *kruttos (“round object”): Welsh crwth (“hump, hunch”). Compare Galician cruto and Asturian corollu.
Unknown. Probably from a substrate term *tǒrgăno-; cognate of Leonese and Asturian tuérganu.

parole.significato: trunk and roots of heather, traditionally used in the production of coal
parole.testo: Unknown. Probably from a substrate term *tǒrgăno-; cognate of Leonese and Asturian tuérgano.

parole.significato: ankle (each of the bony protrusions (external and internal) that are found in the region of the joint between the leg a…
parole.testo: From Middle Portuguese tormezelo, from Old Galician-Portuguese, from *turmo (“bulk, swelling”) + -celo, from a substrate language. Cognate with Galician tornecelo and probably with Catalan turmell and Occitan turmel.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: snail (any animal of the class Gastropoda having a shell)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from a derivation of Vulgar Latin *cochleār, Latin cochlea (“snail”), from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”). Compare with colher (“spoon”). Alternatively, possibly of pre-Roman substrate origin. Cognate with Galician, Asturian, and Spanish caracol, Catalan
Unknown. Possibly from a pre-Roman Paleo-Hispanic substrate, or from North Germanic/Scandinavian flark. Compare Spanish charco, from which it could have been borrowed.

parole.significato: throat (posterior region of the oral cavity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese garganta; from a substrate language *gʷr̥h₃gn̥t- (“throat”), cognate with Proto-Celtic *brāgants (“neck, throat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”). Alternatively, onomatopoeic.
